intro: Imagine you have a box with 10 toys and you want to find your red car. You look at the toys one by one. Now imagine the box has 10,000 toys. It takes a lot longer, right? **Algorithm analysis** is the science of predicting **how much longer** a program takes when the amount of data gets bigger, before we even run it.

An [[algorithm|a list of clear steps that solves a problem, like a recipe]] can be fast with 10 items and painfully slow with a million. Phone maps, video search, online shops and games all depend on programmers who choose the steps that keep growing slowly. The tool they use to talk about this is called **Big O**.

In this summary you will learn: how to describe growth with Big O and its cousins, how to count the steps of loops, how to solve the equations of recursive algorithms, how to prove that an algorithm is correct, why some costs are better than they look (amortised analysis), why sorting has a speed limit, how much memory an algorithm needs, how fast the common data structures are, and what the famous question P versus NP is about. At the end you will be ready for the quiz.

sections.title: The big picture: what do we measure?

blocks.text: When you ask 'how fast is this program?', the answer in seconds is not very useful. A fast computer and a slow computer give different seconds for the same program. So we count something that does not change: the number of **basic steps** (a comparison, an addition, reading one cell of memory) as a function of the **input size**, which we call `n`.

Think of a teacher who gives back homework. If she has `n` notebooks and handles each one once, the work grows in step with `n`. If she compares every notebook with every other notebook, the work grows much faster. We do not care if she is quick or slow: we care how the work grows.
Two kinds of cost

rows: How many basic steps does it take?
Looking at every item of a list: about n steps
How much extra memory does it need?
Making a copy of the list: about n extra cells

blocks.text: Words you will meet

items: **Input size (n)**: how much data the algorithm receives, for example the number of items in a list.
**[[Asymptotic|what happens when n becomes very, very large]]**: we look at the big picture for huge inputs and ignore small details.
**Order of growth**: the 'shape' of the growth, such as 'straight line' or 'curve that shoots up'.
**Worst, best and average case**: the cost for the unluckiest input, the luckiest input, and a typical input.
**Lower bound**: a limit saying 'no algorithm can do better than this'.

blocks.text: Big O does not measure seconds. It measures how the number of steps grows when the input grows.

sections.title: Growth of functions and their ordering

blocks.text: Different algorithms grow in different ways. Some barely notice a bigger input. Others explode. To compare them we use a small family of 'speeds', from the gentlest to the wildest.

rows: Opening the first page of a book: it does not matter how thick the book is
Finding a word in a dictionary by opening it in the middle and halving the search again and again
Slow growth, but faster than log n
Sorting a deck of cards in a clever way
Every student shaking hands with every other student
Every new item doubles the work
Trying every possible order of n items
blocks.caption: From slowest growth (top) to fastest growth (bottom)

blocks.text: The order is: **1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ**. A '[[logarithm|log2 n answers: how many times can I cut n in half until only 1 is left?]]' grows very slowly: log₂ 1,024 is only 10, and log₂ 1,000,000 is only about 20.

blocks.title: Steps needed for n = 16 under each growth

blocks.text: What happens when the input doubles?

rows: gets squared: it is not even close to manageable

blocks.text: Two useful facts for comparing. First, **polynomial** growth (a power of n, like n² or n^1.5) always loses against **exponential** growth (2ⁿ) for big n. Second, a power of `log n`, even `(log n)¹⁰`, always loses against a small power of n like `√n` for big n. So n log n is smaller than n^1.5, because log n grows more slowly than √n. And `n / log n` is smaller than `n`, but larger than `√n`.

A faster computer helps less than you think. If an algorithm does n² operations and today it solves n = 1,000 in one second, a machine **100 times faster** solves only n = 10,000 in that second (because 10,000² = 100 × 1,000²). The same speed-up on a 2ⁿ algorithm adds only about 7 to n.
A 'bad' growth can still win for small inputs. 100n is slower than n² when n is below 100; from n > 100 on, 100n does strictly fewer operations. That is why we say 'for large n'.
Order to memorise: 1, log n, √n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ, n!. A faster machine does not change the order of growth.

sections.title: Asymptotic notation: O, Ω, Θ, o, ω

blocks.text: Suppose an algorithm does exactly 3n² + 10n + 5 steps. For a huge n, the 10n and the 5 are tiny compared with 3n², and the 3 only depends on the computer. So we say the algorithm is 'of order n²'. The notations below give a precise way to say that.
Compare two numbers a and b. You can say a ≤ b, a ≥ b, a = b, a < b or a > b. The five notations do the same for functions that describe growth.

rows: f grows at most as fast as g (upper bound)
f grows at least as fast as g (lower bound)
f grows at the same rate as g (tight bound)
f grows strictly slower than g
f grows strictly faster than g

blocks.text: The formal definition (for non-negative functions)

**f(n) = O(g(n))** means: there are constants `c > 0` and `n0` such that `f(n) ≤ c · g(n)` for every `n ≥ n0`. In words: after some point, f never goes above a constant multiple of g. **Ω** is the same with `≥`. **Θ** needs both: f = Θ(g) exactly when f = O(g) **and** f = Ω(g).
Example: to show 100n + 50 = O(n), take c = 150 and n0 = 1. For n ≥ 1 we have 100n + 50 ≤ 100n + 50n = 150n. Another valid pair is c = 101 and n0 = 50. Any pair that works proves the statement.

With limits it is even easier. Look at the ratio f(n)/g(n) when n goes to infinity. If it tends to **0**, then f = o(g). If it tends to **infinity**, then f = ω(g). If it tends to a **positive constant** (for example 7), then f = Θ(g).

blocks.content:
ratio f(n)/g(n) when n -> infinity

  0               ->  f = o(g)     (f is smaller)
  constant > 0    ->  f = Θ(g)     (same rate)
  infinity        ->  f = ω(g)     (f is bigger)
blocks.caption: Using the ratio to compare growth

blocks.text: Useful facts

items: **n = O(n²) is true.** O is only an upper bound, it does not need to be tight. It is like saying 'I am less than 100 years old'.
**Ω alone says nothing about an upper bound.** 'This takes at least n steps' could be n or 1,000,000 n.
**2^(n+1) = Θ(2ⁿ)**, because 2^(n+1) = 2 · 2ⁿ is only a constant factor bigger. But **2^(2n) = 4ⁿ = ω(2ⁿ)**, because the ratio 2ⁿ goes to infinity.
**The base of a logarithm does not matter** inside O. log₂ n and log₁₀ n differ by a constant factor, so we just write O(log n).
**Θ is symmetric**: if f = Θ(g), then g = Θ(f). O is not: n = O(n²), but n² is not O(n).
**log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n)**. This sum of logarithms is the tight order of growth of the logarithm of a factorial.
Some pairs of functions are **not comparable**. If f(n) = n and g(n) is 1 for even n but n² for odd n, then f is neither O(g) nor Ω(g).

blocks.text: Do not confuse the notation with the case. Insertion sort takes about n steps on a sorted list and about n² on a reversed list. For all inputs of size n we can only say its time is Ω(n) and O(n²). It is not Θ(n²) for all inputs, and not Θ(n) for all inputs.
O is ≤, Ω is ≥, Θ is =, o is <, ω is >. We drop constants and smaller terms: 3n² + 10n + 5 is Θ(n²).
To find the Big O of a program, we count how many times its main line runs as a function of `n`. A few rules solve almost every case.

items: **One after the other: add.** Two loops one after the other, each with n steps, cost n + n = 2n, which is Θ(n).
**One inside the other: multiply.** A loop of n steps containing another loop of n steps costs n × n = n².
**Drop constants and smaller terms.** n² + n is Θ(n²).
**An if / else: take the worst branch** when you do not know which one will be used.

blocks.text: Single loops and nested loops

blocks.caption: Pairs of positions: n(n-1)/2

blocks.text: Counting pairs is like counting handshakes in a room of n people: every pair shakes hands once, so there are n(n-1)/2 handshakes. Counting triples i < j < k works the same way: n(n-1)(n-2)/6 triples. For n = 6 that is 20. This is Θ(n³).
Loops that double or step by a changing amount

blocks.caption: Three loops that do not cost n²

blocks.text: The middle example is a **geometric sum**: each term is double the one before, so the whole sum is about twice the last term. The last example is a **harmonic sum**: n/1 + n/2 + ... + n/n, which is n times about ln n.
The cost depends on the value, not only on the length

A simple primality test tries divisors d = 2, 3, 4... while d × d ≤ n. In the worst case it makes about **√n** divisions, where n is the **value** being tested. That looks gentle, but a number with 100 digits has a value around 10¹⁰⁰, so √n is 10⁵⁰: far too many. Measured against the **number of digits**, the cost is exponential.

Look at the loop limits, not only at how many loops there are. Two nested loops can be Θ(n²), Θ(n log n) or even Θ(n). And a loop that runs n times with an if inside costs, at worst, n times the worst branch: if one branch is Θ(n), the total is O(n²).
Sequence: add. Nesting: multiply. Halving or doubling: log n. Drop constants. For an if, assume the worst branch.

The same algorithm can behave very differently depending on the data it receives. Looking for a name in a list of n names: if it is the first one you are lucky, if it is the last one (or missing) you are unlucky.

rows: The cheapest input of size n
The most expensive input of size n: a guarantee
The expected cost over a set of inputs
(n + 1) / 2 comparisons if the item is present and every position is equally likely

blocks.text: The **worst case** is the one we use most, because it is a promise: 'it will never be slower than this'. The **average case** needs an extra assumption that the worst case does not: a **probability distribution** of the inputs (for example, 'all positions are equally likely'). Without that assumption, 'average' means nothing.

The case and the notation are different ideas. Best, worst and average are about the input. O, Ω and Θ are about the growth of a function. You can use any notation with any case: 'the worst case is Θ(n²)' or 'the best case is O(n)'.
Insertion sort

Insertion sort puts each new card in its place among the cards you already hold. On an **already sorted** list each card needs only one comparison: best case Θ(n). On a **reversed** list each card must pass all the previous ones: worst case Θ(n²).
Quicksort and its pivot

Quicksort picks a **pivot**, puts smaller items on one side and bigger on the other, and repeats on each side. If the pivot is always the **first element**, an already sorted (or reversed) list is the worst case: the pivot is the smallest item, one side is empty and the other has n - 1 items. The work is n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... = Θ(n²).

With a **random pivot**, no particular input is bad any more. The bad luck now comes from the random choice, not from the data. The **expected** time is Θ(n log n) for every input. Bad pivots can still happen, but they are rare.

blocks.content:
sorted list, pivot = first element:

[1 2 3 4 5]   pivot 1 -> left: []     right: [2 3 4 5]
[2 3 4 5]     pivot 2 -> left: []     right: [3 4 5]
[3 4 5]       pivot 3 -> left: []     right: [4 5]
...
n levels, each one doing about n work -> Θ(n²)
blocks.caption: Why the first pivot is a bad idea on sorted data
Merge sort has the same order in every case

blocks.text: Worst case = a guarantee. Average case = needs a probability assumption. Randomising the pivot makes the expected time good for every input.

Some algorithms solve a problem by solving **smaller copies of the same problem**. This is called [[recursion|a function that calls itself on a smaller input]]. To measure them we write an equation that says: 'the cost of size n equals the cost of the smaller pieces plus the extra work'. This equation is a **recurrence**.

A teacher splits a pile of 1,000 tests between two helpers. Each helper splits their half again, and so on. At the end, the teachers collect the results. The cost is the cost of the two halves plus the cost of collecting.
Writing the recurrences you need

rows: Binary search (look at the middle, keep one half)
Merge sort (sort two halves, merge in linear time)
Scan then recurse on n - 1 items

blocks.text: For T(n) = T(n-1) + n with T(1) = 1, the values are T(2) = 3, T(3) = 6, T(4) = 10, T(5) = 15. It is the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2. In Hanoi, to move n disks you move n-1 disks, move the biggest disk, and move the n-1 disks again, so the work doubles with every extra disk: T(n) = 2ⁿ - 1.
The master theorem

Many divide-and-conquer recurrences look like **T(n) = a · T(n/b) + f(n)**. Here **a** is the number of recursive calls, **n/b** is the size of each call, and **f(n)** is the extra work outside the calls (splitting and merging). Compare f(n) with the number **n^(log_b a)**, which is how much work the 'leaves' of the recursion do.

rows: f(n) is polynomially smaller than n^(log_b a)
A tie: every level costs the same
f(n) is polynomially bigger than n^(log_b a) (and a regularity condition holds)

blocks.text: 'Polynomially' means by a factor of at least n^ε for some ε > 0. Examples: **T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n**: here n^(log₂ 2) = n and f = n, a tie, so Θ(n log n). **T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n**: n^(log₂ 4) = n² beats n, so Θ(n²). **T(n) = T(n/2) + n**: n^(log₂ 1) = 1, f = n is bigger, so Θ(n). **Strassen: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n²**: n^(log₂ 7) is about n^2.81, which beats n², so Θ(n^(log₂ 7)).

blocks.content:
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

depth 0:      [ n ]                       -> n
depth 1:   [n/2]   [n/2]                  -> n
depth 2: [n/4][n/4][n/4][n/4]             -> n
...
depth i: 2^i nodes of size n/2^i          -> n

levels: log2(n)   total = n * log2(n)
blocks.caption: A recursion tree: every level costs n

blocks.text: The **recursion tree** shows why. At depth i there are 2^i nodes, each costing n / 2^i, so every level adds up to **n**. With about log n levels the total is n log n.
When the master theorem does not apply

items: **T(n) = T(n-1) + n** and **T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1**: the subproblem is n - 1, not n divided by something. Use the recursion tree, or expand and add.
**T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n**: f(n) is bigger than n, but not **polynomially** bigger, so it falls between the three basic cases. An extended version gives Θ(n log² n).
**T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n**: the two calls have different sizes. The recursion tree has about log n levels, each costing at most n, and the answer is Θ(n log n).

blocks.text: Proving by substitution

Another method is to **guess** the answer and **prove it by induction**. Careful: you must prove exactly the statement you guessed. If you assume T(n/2) ≤ c · n/2 for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, you get T(n) ≤ cn + n. That is **not** ≤ cn, so the proof of T(n) = O(n) fails (and indeed T(n) is Θ(n log n)). Concluding 'cn + n is O(n)' is a classic mistake, because the constant c must stay the same.
Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a): smaller means leaves win, equal means multiply by log n, bigger means the root wins.

sections.title: Loop invariants and proof of correctness

blocks.text: Being fast is useless if the answer is wrong. A **loop invariant** is a sentence about the variables that is **true every time the loop starts a new round**. It is a way of proving that an algorithm does the right thing.

A train with n cars is being checked, one car at a time. At every moment you can say: 'all the cars behind me are already checked'. That sentence is true at the beginning (zero cars behind), stays true after each step, and at the end it says the whole train is checked. That sentence is the invariant.
The three steps

rows: The invariant is true before the first round
If it is true before a round, it is still true after it
When the loop stops, the invariant plus the stop condition give the result we want
Using the result at the end (induction alone has no 'end')

blocks.caption: Sum of an array

blocks.text: Insertion sort has a famous invariant: at the start of the round that inserts a[j], the part a[0..j-1] holds the **same elements as at the beginning, in sorted order**. When j reaches n, the whole array is sorted.
A good invariant is strong enough

For a loop that computes the maximum with m = a[0], the sentence 'm equals some element of the array' is always true, but it is **useless**: at the end it does not say m is the largest. The right invariant is 'm is the largest of a[0..i-1]'. In termination, i = n and so m is the largest of the whole array.
Correct is not the same as finishing

An invariant proves that **if** the loop ends, the answer is right. You must also prove that the loop **ends**. In binary search, if lo = mid + 1 is changed to lo = mid, the invariant 'if x is in the array it is in a[lo..hi]' is still true, but when hi = lo + 1 the value of mid does not change and the loop runs forever. To prove termination, show a quantity that gets smaller each round and cannot go below a limit (here, hi - lo).
A true sentence is not automatically a good invariant. It must be true at the start, kept by every round, and strong enough to give the final result, and the loop must end.
Initialisation, maintenance, termination. Base case, inductive step, and use the result at the end.

Some operations are cheap most of the time and expensive once in a while. If we only looked at the worst single operation we would be too pessimistic. **Amortised analysis** gives the **average cost of an operation over a whole sequence of operations** in the worst case. No probability is involved: it is a guarantee about the sequence.
Imagine paying a yearly bus pass of 120 dollars once. A single day costs 120, but over the year each day costs about 0.33. The expensive payment is spread over many cheap days.
The dynamic array that doubles

A [[dynamic array|a list that grows: when it is full, it gets a bigger home and copies everything there]] has some capacity. Appending to a full array is expensive because all elements are copied to a new array of **double** the capacity. Starting with capacity 1, after 16 appends the copies were 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = **15** in total (the 17th append would copy 16 more). The sum of the copies is always less than 2n, so each append costs **O(1) amortised**.

blocks.content:
capacity:  1   2   4       8               16
append #:  1   2  3 4,5 ... 8,9 ....... 16,17
copies:    -   1   2   4              8      (grow when full)

total copies after 16 appends = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15
blocks.caption: Doubling: the copies add up to less than 2n

blocks.text: If instead we grow by a **fixed amount** (say +100 slots), the copies are n + (n-100) + (n-200) + ... which is about n²/200 in total. That is **Θ(n²) for n appends**, so each append costs O(n) amortised. Doubling (growing by a factor) is what makes it O(1).
The binary counter

A binary counter flips bits when it increments. The lowest bit flips every time, the next every 2 increments, the next every 4... For a 5-bit counter incremented 16 times the flips are 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = **31**, less than 2 per increment. So an increment costs **O(1) amortised**, even though one increment can flip all the bits.
Methods

items: **Aggregate method**: add up the cost of all n operations and divide by n (what we did above).

**Accounting (banker's) method**: charge each operation a fixed price. Cheap operations are charged more than they cost, and the extra goes into a bank as **credit**. Expensive operations are paid for with the credit. The bank must never go negative.
**Potential method**: a more formal version of the same idea, with a 'potential energy' stored in the data structure.

blocks.text: Shrinking too eagerly breaks the guarantee. If an array doubles when full but halves as soon as it is half empty, then alternating insert and delete near the boundary makes it grow and shrink all the time, and each operation can cost Θ(n). The usual fix is to shrink only when it is a quarter full.
Amortised O(1) means: any sequence of n operations costs O(n) in total, even if one single operation is expensive. It is a worst-case guarantee, not an average over random inputs.

sections.title: The lower bound of comparison sorting

blocks.text: Until now we looked for faster algorithms. Now we ask: is there a **speed limit** that no sorting algorithm can beat? For algorithms that sort by **comparing** two items at a time (like merge sort, quicksort and heap sort), the answer is yes: **Ω(n log n)**.

It is the game of 'twenty questions'. Each question has only two answers (yes or no). To tell apart 1,000,000 possible things you need at least 20 questions, because 20 yes/no questions give at most 2²⁰ ≈ 1,000,000 different outcomes.
The decision tree

Draw every comparison the algorithm makes as a branch: 'is a < b?' goes left for yes and right for no. Each path from the root to a leaf is one run of the algorithm, and the leaf says which order was found. For n distinct items there are **n!** possible orders, and every one must appear as a leaf. So the tree has at least **n! leaves**.

blocks.content:
sorting 3 items a, b, c  (3! = 6 orders = 6 leaves)

            a < b ?
          /         \
     b < c ?       a < c ?
     /     \       /     \
  abc    a<c?    bac    b<c?
         /  \           /  \
       acb  cab       bca  cba
blocks.caption: A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves

blocks.text: A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves. So 2^h ≥ n!, and the height satisfies **h ≥ log₂(n!)**. The height is the number of comparisons in the worst case. And log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n). Therefore any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

blocks.title: Minimum comparisons needed in the worst case (ceiling of log2 of n!)

blocks.text: For 4 items: 4! = 24 orders, and 2⁴ = 16 < 24 ≤ 32 = 2⁵, so at least **5 comparisons** are needed. For 5 items: 5! = 120 > 2⁶ = 64, so nobody can sort 5 items with 6 comparisons in the worst case: such a claim cannot be true.
How can some sorts be faster?
The bound applies only to sorts that learn about the data **by comparing**. Sorts that use the **values themselves** escape it:

rows: For integers from 0 to k - 1: count how many times each value appears
d digits, each with k possible values: sort digit by digit with a stable counting sort

blocks.text: They do not contradict the bound because they never ask 'is a < b?'. They use the value as an index in a table. The price: the range k must be small, and they only work for things like integers or short keys.
Comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case (n! leaves, height at least log₂ n!). Merge sort is optimal. Counting and radix sort are not comparison sorts, so they can be linear.

Time is not the only thing that costs. An algorithm also uses memory. **Space complexity** measures the memory an algorithm needs as the input grows. We usually count the **auxiliary space**: the extra memory used on top of the input itself.
To sort a pile of cards, you can swap cards in place on the table (almost no extra space), or copy them to a second table while you work (another n cards of space).

rows: A few variables, no matter how big the array is
It needs a second array to merge into
O(log n) on average, O(n) worst case
Space comes from the recursion stack
n calls waiting on the stack
Exponential calls, but only one chain at a time on the stack

blocks.text: **O(1) auxiliary space** means a fixed number of extra variables, not growing with n. Careful: 'in place' with recursion still uses space, because every call that has not finished is kept in the **call stack**. If a function calls itself n times in a chain, the stack holds n calls: O(n).

blocks.caption: Recursion costs stack space

blocks.text: Quicksort partitions in place, but it recurses on both sides. If the pivot is always the worst one, the chain of calls is n deep, so the stack is O(n). Fibonacci with two calls makes an exponential number of calls in total, but at any single moment only one path from the root is open, at most n calls deep, so the stack is O(n).

There is also a link with time. If every step touches a constant number of memory cells, an algorithm cannot use more cells than it has steps. So **S(n) = O(T(n))**: the space is never bigger than the time. The opposite is false: an algorithm can take a lot of time using almost no memory.
Auxiliary space is the extra memory beyond the input. Recursion depth counts. Space is never bigger than time, but time can be much bigger than space.

sections.title: Complexity of common data structure operations

blocks.text: Choosing a data structure is choosing which operations are cheap. Here are the costs you should know, with n elements.

rows: Read position i: O(1). Search by value: O(n)
Fast to read, slow to open a gap
O(1) if you have the node before it
Fast to insert at the front
Great for reading, bad for changing
Hash table (good hash, controlled load factor)
Worst case O(n) if all keys collide in one list
Also lists keys in order in O(n)
Building a heap from n items: O(n)

blocks.text: Let us see why some of these hold.
Arrays and linked lists

An array keeps items side by side, so position i is found by simple arithmetic: O(1). But inserting at the beginning pushes every item one place to the right: O(n). A linked list is a chain of boxes, each pointing to the next, so inserting at the beginning only changes one pointer: O(1). To reach the i-th box you have to walk the chain: O(n).
Hash tables

A [[hash table|a table where a function turns each key into the number of a drawer, so you open the right drawer directly]] with a good hash function and a controlled **load factor** (items per drawer) finds a key in **O(1) on average**. With chaining (each drawer holds a list), if every key falls into the same drawer, the lookup walks one list of n keys: **O(n) in the worst case**.
Trees and heaps

A binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and bigger on the right. If you insert 1, 2, 3, ..., n in order into a **plain tree with no balancing**, every key goes to the right, and the tree becomes a list: searching for n costs **O(n)**. A balanced tree (AVL, red-black) repairs itself and keeps the height at O(log n), so it gives O(log n) search, insert and remove in the worst case, **and** an in-order walk lists the keys sorted in O(n). A hash table cannot list keys in order, so only the balanced tree meets all these requirements.

A binary min-heap keeps the smallest item at the root: reading it is O(1), removing it is O(log n) (move the last item to the root and let it sink). Building a heap from an arbitrary array with sift-down from the last internal node up to the root costs only **O(n)**, not O(n log n), because most nodes are near the bottom and sink very little.
A queue on an array

If a queue is an array, enqueue writes at the end (O(1) amortised) but dequeue removes index 0 and shifts all the others: O(n). For n enqueues and n dequeues the total is **O(n²)**. A linked list, or an array with two indices that move (a circular buffer), brings each operation to O(1).

blocks.title: Steps to look for the last key among n = 1,024 keys

blocks.text: Array: O(1) read, O(n) insert at the front. List: O(1) insert at the front, O(n) read. Hash: O(1) average, O(n) worst. Balanced tree: O(log n) and ordered. Heap: O(1) minimum, O(log n) removal, O(n) build.
So far every algorithm we saw is 'fast enough'. But some problems seem to have no fast algorithm at all. To talk about them, computer scientists sort problems into **classes**.
Polynomial and non-polynomial

An algorithm runs in **polynomial time** if its cost is bounded by n raised to a fixed power: n, n log n, n², n³⁰⁰... Algorithms like 2ⁿ or n! are **not polynomial** (they are exponential or worse). Even n^(log n) is not polynomial. Polynomial algorithms are called **tractable** (manageable). The others are **intractable** for big inputs: even a computer a million times faster does not rescue 2ⁿ.
The classes

rows: Problems that can be **solved** in polynomial time
Problems whose proposed answer can be **checked** in polynomial time
Someone shows you a solved sudoku: checking is quick
The hardest problems in NP: every problem in NP can be turned into them
At least as hard as every problem in NP (may not even be in NP)
Hard, and maybe not even checkable

blocks.text: Solving a puzzle can take hours, but looking at a finished puzzle and seeing that it is correct takes seconds. NP is the class of problems that are easy to check, even if they may be hard to solve.

blocks.caption: The picture if P is different from NP

blocks.text: Facts you need

items: **P ⊆ NP**: if you can solve a problem fast, you can also check an answer fast.
**P = NP is an open question.** Nobody has proved it, and nobody has proved the opposite. Most experts believe P ≠ NP, but this is a belief, not a theorem.

A **decision problem** has a yes/no answer. The travelling salesman decision version asks: 'is there a tour visiting all n cities once and returning to the start with cost at most K?'. It is in NP because, given a tour, you check in polynomial time that it visits every city once and that the cost is at most K.
If anyone finds a polynomial algorithm for **one** NP-complete problem (such as SAT, the satisfiability of logic formulas), then **every** problem in NP has one, and P = NP.

To prove a new problem X is **NP-hard**, take a problem A already known to be NP-complete and build a **polynomial-time reduction** from A to X: a fast way to turn any instance of A into an instance of X with the same answer. If X were easy, A would be easy.

blocks.text: Note the direction of the reduction: you reduce the **known hard** problem **to the new one**. Doing it backwards (new problem to known problem) would only show that the new problem is not harder than A, which proves nothing about its hardness.
NP does not mean 'not polynomial'. It means 'nondeterministic polynomial': solutions are checkable in polynomial time. Every problem in P is also in NP.
P: solved fast. NP: checked fast. NP-complete: the hardest in NP; one fast algorithm for any of them would give P = NP. Reductions go from the known hard problem to the new one.
All the tools of this area answer one question: how does the cost of an algorithm grow with the size of the input? Here is how the pieces connect.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Thinking that Big O gives time in seconds. It gives the shape of growth.
Confusing the best, worst and average case with the notations O, Ω and Θ.
Saying Θ when you only proved O.
Forgetting to drop constants and smaller terms, or dropping a term that matters (for example inside an exponent).
Ignoring the memory used by recursion.
Using the master theorem when the recurrence does not have the form a · T(n/b) + f(n).
Believing that a faster computer changes the order of growth.
Reading NP as 'not polynomial'.

blocks.text: When you see a question, first decide: is it about growth (notation), counting (loops or recurrences), correctness (invariants), cost over a sequence (amortised), a limit (lower bound, P and NP) or memory (space)? Then use the right tool. You can read more in [Khan Academy: asymptotic notation](https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/computer-science/algorithms/asymptotic-notation/a/asymptotic-notation) and the [Big-O Cheat Sheet](https://www.bigocheatsheet.com/).
Count the steps, ignore the constants, look at the big picture for large n, and always say which case and which notation you mean.
